definition: Diminutive means remarkably or extremely small in size.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word diminutive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know diminutive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Next to the towering draft horses, the diminutive pony at the county fair looked like a plush toy that had wandered out of the gift shop.
Something small is simply below average size, while something diminutive is so remarkably small that its size is the first thing you notice.
A diminutive object is strikingly tiny but still easy to see, whereas a microscopic one is too small to see without special equipment.

Tiny simply means extremely small, and it is the plain, everyday word: a tiny crumb, a tiny apartment. Diminutive adds a note of surprise or affection at how remarkably small something is for its kind, the way a diminutive pony stands out beside full-sized horses.

Minuscule means so small it is hard to notice at all: a minuscule typo, a minuscule speck of dust. Diminutive things are strikingly small but still plainly visible; their smallness is the first thing you see, not something you strain to find.

Miniature means made as a much smaller copy of something larger, like dollhouse furniture or a model train. A miniature is small on purpose, by design. Diminutive describes a real thing that happens to be remarkably small for its kind, not a scaled-down replica.

Diminutive means remarkably or extremely small in size.
The harbor pilot climbed aboard the diminutive tugboat, a vessel dwarfed by the container ship it had come to guide.
Onlookers on the pier marveled that a boat so strikingly small could steer a giant hundreds of times its weight safely into port.
The tugboat's strikingly small size next to the enormous container ship is exactly what diminutive describes: remarkable smallness that you notice at a glance.
formal, often admiring or affectionate

Diminutive describes physical size and often carries a tone of surprise or affection, as in 'the diminutive gymnast' or 'a diminutive cottage.' In grammar, a diminutive is also a word form that signals smallness, such as duckling from duck.
Keep it for the visible size of things and creatures, not for small amounts or quantities.

Every harbor has a favorite boat, and in Port Alba it is the Maribel, a ferry half the length of any other vessel on the commuter run.
Tourists photograph her beside the steel giants at the pier; regulars pat her rail like the flank of a well-loved dog.
The harbor guide calls her the diminutive queen of the morning crossing.
A new harbormaster once proposed retiring her, arguing that so small a boat must be a relic.
The Maribel, they pointed out, threads the narrow channel no full-sized ferry can enter, and she has missed two mornings in thirty years.
The harbormaster gave in, and the next schedule listed her first — small for her kind, and cherished for it.
